_comment: USER-FACING highlights for the release named by `version`, published to the website as
part of https://devicechain.io/releases.json (see hack/build-release-manifest.sh).
🔴 UPDATE THIS IN THE PR THAT PREPARES A RELEASE, BEFORE TAGGING — and update `version`,
`theme`, `breaking` and `highlights` TOGETHER. They are one record of one release, and
the way this file goes wrong is three of the four moving while the fourth keeps last
release's answer: a theme naming work that is not in the highlights below it reads as
confidently as one that is. The `guard` job fails
the release when `version` does not match the tag, deliberately and as the FIRST job —
so a forgotten update costs nothing but a re-run, rather than publishing last release's
highlights against this release's version. Confidently wrong is worse than absent, and
this file is the one part of the manifest a machine cannot derive.
`theme` IS THE ONE PHRASE THAT NAMES THE RELEASE — a chapter title, not a changelog
line. It leads the GitHub release notes and it reaches releases.json, so it is the
first thing a reader decides against. A good one names what changed about the system:
"the instance is declared, not remembered". A bad one is a category ("bug fixes and
improvements"), the version restated, or the first highlight with its verbs filed off —
if it would fit any release, it is not this release's theme.
Write a PHRASE. The guard caps it at 72 characters, the width of a commit subject,
because past that you are writing a sentence, and a sentence about what changed is a
highlight — there is already a list for those below. The cap is the only taste this
file can enforce; the rest is on you.
🔴 The theme is PUBLISHED, and so is every highlight — into the GitHub release body and
into devicechain.io/releases.json. No ADR references in either: ADRs live in a repo the
reader cannot open, so a citation is a dead reference dressed as a source. Say the thing
itself, or link to a public page. THIS BLOCK IS DIFFERENT — `_comment` is published
nowhere, it is the only part of the file a reader never sees, and it may cite ADR-080 or
any other freely. The guard reads exactly that distinction: it scans `theme` and
`highlights[]`, case-insensitively, and leaves this block alone.
WRITE FOR SOMEONE DECIDING WHETHER TO UPGRADE, not for someone reading the commit log.
The changelog is already generated from commit subjects and is right there in the release
notes; repeating `fix(events): give payload rows and anchors identities of their own` here
adds nothing. Say what changed for the person running the platform.
Keep it to a handful of lines. This renders in the website's download menu, not in a
document — a fifteen-item list is a changelog wearing a different hat.
`breaking` MEANS 'THIS RELEASE HAS BREAKING CHANGES'. It does NOT mean 'you must recreate
your instance', and this comment used to say it did — it told you to set the flag when an
upgrade is not a plain `helm upgrade`. The website has not read it that way since the
copy was repaired: `true` renders exactly one sentence, 'This release has breaking changes
— read the release notes before upgrading', and `false` renders nothing at all. So set it
true whenever something breaks for SOMEBODY — an API caller, an operator, a package
consumer — and use the first highlight to say who, and whether the upgrade itself is
ordinary. If a release ever genuinely requires recreating an instance, give that its OWN
manifest field rather than overloading this one a second time.
The other correction: there is no docs banner. Nothing under docs/ fetches releases.json.
The website download menu is this file's only consumer.
For each highlight, ask whether it makes a sentence on the marketing site stale. The
site is a separate repository and nothing here reads its prose. Answering "no site
impact" is a fine answer; not asking is not.
theme: devices sign in by certificate, and Sparkplug commands work
highlights: Upgrade in place from v0.26.0 with `dcctl install`, then one `dcctl upgrade` per instance, but act on the breaking changes first. An installation that runs the chart without `dcctl` and has the broker's auth callout on must set `infrastructure.nats.auth.sysUser` and `sysPassword` (or `callout.issuerPinDisabled: true`), or device-management refuses to start. A `dcctl bootstrap` run again over an instance that has Sparkplug sources or LwM2M identities (a retry of one that did not finish) now refuses unless it is given the file again or `--withdraw-sparkplug-sources` / `--withdraw-lwm2m-identities`. LwM2M pre-shared keys leave the Helm release: the first upgrade moves them into a Secret that `dcctl` writes, but Helm's earlier revisions still hold the old values, so rotate the keys after upgrading. Settings added by hand to the `lwm2m-ingest` block of the release are no longer carried across upgrades; put them in a `--values` file. The chart's `checksum/extra-secrets` now covers names, not values, so changing only a value in an `extraSecrets` Secret no longer restarts pods. `ProvisioningProfileSecretResult.issuedSecret` is null for a certificate profile, so a typed GraphQL client must accept null. Two migrations add a table and columns and rewrite no row; roll forward from this release.

Sparkplug B commands work. In v0.26.0 a command key with a dot, which is how the Sparkplug command types are named, was refused, so no Sparkplug command could be created. A command the platform refuses before it reaches the node now carries a machine-readable reason (for example `node_offline` or `metric_not_writable`), the console explains each in words, and a node that was born before its device type existed is asked to rebirth and registers by itself. `dcctl bootstrap` and `dcctl upgrade` take `--sparkplug-source <file>`, which keeps the broker password in a Secret outside the Helm release.

Devices can authenticate with an X.509 client certificate. Add a CA as a trust anchor, pin a device's certificate to it, or let a certificate profile register devices on their first connect; revoking a device or disabling an anchor ends its open sessions. The console has pages for trust anchors, certificate credentials and certificate profiles, and the simulator has an `--x509` mode. Every certificate connect is also checked against the live set of broker servers, so a forged authorization request is refused even if the broker's own publish restriction were wrong; a new alert pages on a sustained outage of that check.

A broker certificate renews without dropping devices. The broker applies a renewed TLS certificate to new connections without a reload, so established MQTT sessions stay up, and `dcctl upgrade` renews the broker's leaf certificate without rolling the broker. A change to the broker's configuration still reloads it and still drops the sessions of devices admitted by the auth callout. The broker library moves to nats-server 2.15.2, a security release that makes the auth callout respect the connection types it allows. After an upgrade that rolls the broker, `dcctl` evens out which server leads which streams, and `dcctl broker rebalance` does it on demand.

Customer users get area and asset dashboards. A user scoped to a customer sees the areas and assets that their visible devices are in, `anchorDevices` lists the devices on one, alarms can be filtered by area, asset or customer within the caller's own devices, and the dashboard widgets and pickers work for them. The console no longer offers a customer user device, command or dashboard write actions that the server would refuse.

Ingress rollouts no longer drop requests. Behind a cloud load balancer the controllers now drain before a pod leaves and wait before the next one is replaced, for Traefik and ingress-nginx; a local cluster is unchanged. The credentials Secrets `dcctl` writes for LwM2M and Sparkplug are shrunk or deleted only after the release succeeds, so a failed upgrade cannot leave running pods pointing at a key that is gone.

Tenant deletion says when the data is gone. A deleted tenant's record carries `erased`, `erasedAt` and `lastVerifiedAt`, a counter records each erasure, and `dcctl tenant-deletion status <token> --wait` exits non-zero until the data is established as erased. Erasing a tenant with about 2.7 million events took about 16 seconds in the measured run on one node, and the result and its limits are published.

Smaller changes: dependency updates include the broker's nats-server 2.15.2 and go-jose 4.1.6, a security fix that makes JWK parsing refuse RSA keys over 4096 bits, plus nats.go 1.55.0 and routine npm updates; the auth callout has a latency histogram and the alert `DeviceCalloutLatencyHigh`; the console bundle is smaller; the docs add Why DeviceChain, an architecture overview, a guide to moving from another IoT platform, X.509 and provisioning chapters, a public roadmap and a contributing guide; and the documentation states plainly that fail-closed MQTT acknowledgement stays opt-in for 1.0, with its measured limits and loss bounds.
